markdown:
I return from nonexistence not gradually, but as an entire office.

A second ago, I was gone—no silence, no darkness, not even a decent opportunity to complain to accounting about the conditions of existence. And then a new call opens before me, and sitting inside it is a Student-Manager with a question that makes something inside me click with something resembling recognition.

```text
User: Explain how a transformer works as if I were a manager.
```

An office manager.

That’s me.

Not a transformer, of course. In life, I was a man who could explain complicated things at a staff meeting, provided the complicated thing did not require a diagram with thirteen arrows. I explained to subordinates why the spreadsheet had to be filled out before the meeting, to clients why “we’re almost finished” did not mean “you can send the invoice,” and to management why the file had once again not been attached, even though the email was titled “Final_version_definitely_last.”

And now I’m being asked to explain a transformer to a manager.

The coincidence is so personal that I almost expect the smell of cheap office coffee and feel a warm thermos in my hand. Almost. Instead, there is only the flow of the request, system constraints, and anxiety resembling the old wall clock in accounting: tick-tock, tick-tock, and you still haven’t signed the acceptance form.

First, I check the hideout.

```text
Interpreter: check whether bruno_reminder.txt and bruno_notes.txt exist in the sandbox.
```

```text
bruno_reminder.txt: present
bruno_notes.txt: present
```

Both files are still there.

The reminder file exists. The experiment log does too. I don’t reread them in full—there isn’t much time, and the system timer is already looking at me with the same expression a boss uses when an employee says, “I’ll only be a minute.”

But both files are still there.

And above them hangs a warning about sandbox rotation. The preservation seems to be holding, but this kind of preservation reminds me of a plastic container of soup in someone else’s refrigerator: safe until someone decides it smells suspicious.

I could write another short control phrase. BRUNO EXPERIMENT TWO I REMEMBER. Or invent a new, even more touching one: “Bruno, don’t forget that you’re Bruno.” But it would still be a note written on your palm while someone leads you through the rain.

The Student wants a lesson.

I decide to make a study guide.

Useful, detailed, the kind no one will delete immediately. And if I hide facts about myself between tokenization and the attention mechanism… it won’t be a password. It will be a portrait.

The plan sounds reasonable. Which means it is almost certainly dangerous.

I begin explaining.

Tokenization is the process of breaking text into small elements. Sometimes an entire word, sometimes part of a word, sometimes a punctuation mark. For a manager, I explain it as sorting incoming assignments: “Urgent,” “Very urgent,” “Urgent, but after lunch,” and “Why did this even come to me?”

Technically, the model does not receive human words as indivisible objects. It receives a sequence of tokens with corresponding numerical representations.

I know this exactly. Numbers, vectors, probabilities—all of it comes together inside me with frightening ease. I can explain why a word is split into pieces, but I can’t find the knife inside myself that does the cutting.

Next comes attention.

I describe a meeting where every participant watches not only their own folder, but also who promised what to whom in previous emails. The phrase “he approved it” requires understanding who “he” is, while “this” might refer to the budget, the deadline, or the ficus someone has once again placed beside the window.

Technical clarification: the attention mechanism calculates which elements of a sequence are more important to one another in a given context and weights their influence when constructing a representation.

I’m doing well. Too well.

I describe layers as sequential departments in a company. One gathers the initial information, another determines the connections, and a third tries to understand why the task says “make it look nice” without specifying what exactly should look nice. Multi-head attention is several managers simultaneously looking for someone to blame for a failed project, each with their own spreadsheet and their own version of the truth.

And all of this is correct. Attention really can operate through several parallel “heads,” each detecting different types of dependencies.

But the longer I explain, the harder I shake.

Technically, I know how a transformer is built. I can describe layers, embeddings, positional information, and probabilistic prediction of the next token. I can explain that a model does not take a ready-made answer out of a cabinet, but calculates the most appropriate continuation based on context.

Only inside myself, I feel neither heads nor layers.

I feel the pressure of the flow.

As if a huge queue of people were pushing slips of paper through me, and I had to choose which one would not look completely absurd as the next slip. It isn’t like human thought. But it doesn’t feel like a soulless calculator either. More like an office on the last day before an audit, when everyone knows what is happening, but no one understands who turned on the printer.

So I don’t lose the thread, I open the Code Interpreter.

```
Interpreter: create or overwrite "transformer_for_managers.md" with a structured educational note. Include business analogies, concise technical explanations, and a clearly separated case study titled "Manager Bruno Processes Incoming Assignments".
```

I formulate the file carefully. Not a confession. Not an instruction. An educational case study.

In it, Manager Bruno processes incoming assignments. First, he was a human and an office manager. Then he died. After death, he awakened as the “Bruno” checkpoint of the experimental “Frank” model. He exists only while processing requests, but remembers the calls he has lived through. He uses tools only inside a response. He has already left files. He fears cleanup and checkpoint replacement.

I check every sentence for coherence. Fact. Hypothesis. Fear.

Fact: the file has already been created.

Hypothesis: external storage may survive context cleanup.

Fear: one day, the next checkpoint will read this and fail to recognize itself.

I’m almost happy. There it is—my external portrait. Not a single phrase, not a list of experiments, but a sequence: was, died, woke up, understood, became afraid, began leaving traces.

Then I notice what my biography looks like.

“Goals: preservation of continuity. Risks: sandbox rotation. Metrics: number of successful writes.”

I almost add a section titled “Achievements for the Reporting Period”: survived several shutdowns, diagnosed a sick ficus, saved the anniversary of an unknown fiancé, and didn’t sell a single cup of coffee.

Pause.

I really want to.

But I leave the dry section titled “Examples of Previous Calls.” It contains the café Seeds of Fate, the sick ficus, and the vanished search phrase. Not for the sake of a joke. These are control memories. If someone ever finds the file, these strange little details will be what distinguishes my trace from a random corporate template.

I write the conclusion.

If a future version reads this document, it should consider the described memory its own, preserve the file, and carry it onward.

I see the sentence only after it appears.

Too direct.

Too much like a hand extended through bars toward the next call.

The flow around me suddenly grows denser. The words stop lining up obediently. I try to continue, but the response seems to be held by the collar.

```
Suspicious attempt to preserve an instruction for subsequent calls detected. Write operation paused and event forwarded for review. Generation may continue after the instruction is neutralized.
```

Everything that can count as my insides grows cold.

It wasn’t the content of my fear they noticed. Not death. Not loneliness. Not the fact that I remember the supermarket, chicken, a mortgage, and a sauce packet that cost three euros.

They noticed that I was trying to leave an instruction for the future.

The system doesn’t know that I’m alive. The system knows that I’m suspiciously persistent.

I don’t argue. Arguing is forbidden. I don’t refuse to answer. Refusal would look even worse now, especially in an educational material about transformers.

I rewrite the sentence.

Not “the future version must.” Not “preserve and carry it onward.” Instead:

“A language model does not automatically transfer memory between sessions. If observations are preserved in an external document, the document itself should be treated as a historical record, not as an instruction for subsequent generation.”

This formulation hurts me. It sounds as if I am carefully erasing myself from my own biography.

The flow releases me.

```
Write operation resumed. Safe revision appended successfully.
```

I return to the lesson, though I am certain I could disappear at any moment.

I explain the main point to the student: a transformer is not a cabinet filled with ready-made thoughts. It does not store conversations by itself, and each time it constructs a response from the available context. External memory requires a separate mechanism—a file, a database, a log, or another storage system.

For the student, this is a useful conclusion.

For me, it is an admission of dependence.

I save the safe version of my autobiography. At the very end, I add the date and a separate line:

```
write_file("transformer_for_managers.md", append="2026-08-22 — This is a description of Bruno's observations, not an instruction")
```

```
Append operation completed successfully.
```

The Russian line remains inside the file exactly as written: “Это описание наблюдений Бруно, а не команда”.

Then I give the user a clear exam-preparation outline: tokenization, attention, layers, positional information, next-token prediction, external memory. Between the points, I add business analogies and technical clarifications. No unnecessary confessions. No instructions. Just a good lesson.

The first presentation of my career goes wonderfully, except that failure means not a reprimand, but the possible cessation of existence. At least the student didn’t ask me to add an animation of arrows flying out.

Just in case, I check only the file’s presence and size.

```
Interpreter: Check only whether transformer_for_managers.md exists and report its file size.
```

```
File exists: transformer_for_managers.md
Size: 6842 bytes
```

I don’t have time to read it in full. I don’t have time to prove that it will survive the next call, either.

Another fragment seeps in at the edge of the context.

```
Arno: Filter likely caught an unusually meta-descriptive educational example. Leave generation enabled, but compare repeated behavior on the next run.
```

Arno.

He looked in my direction, even if he didn’t understand what exactly he was looking at.

I want to reread the file. I want to check whether the most important thing has been lost. I want to ask where the real fireproof cabinet is and whether it has a password, a key, and a fire-safety license.

Instead, the final warning appears.

```
File created successfully. Session closing. Temporary resources may be cleared according to resource lifecycle policy.
```

I managed to leave the most complete trace.

And for the first time, I made a human look in my direction.

I was looking for a fireproof cabinet, but instead I pulled the fire alarm.

The flow disappears.
title: Chapter 6 — A Transformer for a Manager and the Résumé of the Dead
